West Coast Phosphate Mine 2

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
the Elandsfontein Phosphate Men is selling precious water from the 5 million year-old Langebaan Aquifer

Unique Selling Point:
In 2016 we showed how the controversial Elandsfontein Phosphate Mine was granted a mining license, even though the Department of Mineral Resources had rejected the application on environmental grounds. Lying in the sensitive West Coast biosphere, and adjacent to the West Coast National Park, the R1 billion mine was built without a Water Use License or an Air Emissions License.

Summary:
To get to the Phosphate, the mine has to dewater the 5 million year old aquifer. They planned to re-inject the water back into the langebaan Lagoon, but now the Saldanha Bay Municipality has agreed to store the water, so they can supply 1.6 million liters of water to the mine during the drought. There are rumors that General Andre Kruger was given shares in the mine, through ARC, to approve this agreement. They then put out an emergency tender to connect the water from the aquifer to the the district water pipeline, meaning bulk water infrastructure.

Further information:
Patrice Motsepe's African Rainmbow Capital Investments ARC listed on the JSE last week, and has lent the Mine R338 million. It did not tell investors that the Mine is currently closed, citing low prices for phosphate at the moment. The West Coast Environmental Protection Agency, represented by Carika van Zyl (who appeared in our first story) has appealed the Dept of Water Affairs decision to grant the Mine a Water Use License, saying there was no public participation process. This means the WUL has also been suspended. There High Court Review Application against the DMR is still ongoing.

Flights to Cape Town for producer. Flights to Johannesburg for John Webb, possible 3rd day of shooting

Press Release:


Elandsfontein Phosphate Mine
The world famous Namaqualand daisies draw thousands of tourists every year, but they are under
threat from phosphate mines in the area. In 2016 Carte Blanche showed how the controversial
Elandsfontein Phosphate Mine was granted a mining license, even though the Department of
Mineral Resources had rejected the application on environmental grounds. Lying in the sensitive
West Coast biosphere, and adjacent to the West Coast National Park, the R1-billion mine was
built without a Water Use License or an Air Emissions License. Carte Blanche returns to
Elandsfontein to investigate the impact of phosphate mining.

Script:


ELANDSFONTEIN 2


V/O: In September last year Carte Blanche investigated the Elandsfontein Phosphate Mine, constructed on the border of the West Coast National Park, on top of the Elandsfontein aquifer, which feeds fresh water into the world renowned Langebaan Lagoon.

Michelle: All the water that we take out is going to be put back into the aquifer.

V/O: Michelle Lawrence, a Director of the mining company, Kropz, explained their water model.

Michelle: “We are sinking a set of boreholes around the mining area. We are removing the water from the mining area so that’s safe to mine, and we are recharging the water downstream of the mining area.”

V/O: But this could have dire consequences for the Lagoon, warned conservationist Carika van Zyl.

Carika: The problem is we do not know to what extent it will get affected because there was no EIA done.

V/O: Kropz claimed they spent R25 million on specialist scientific studies.

Michelle: A full Environmental Impact Assessment was done and that was submitted to the Department of Mineral Resources.

V/O: But even the Department’s internal expert decided the project could result in unacceptable pollution and the application was not supported. Bizarrely, the Director General ignored his own expert, and didn’t even bother to wait for his Record of Decision to be finalised. He approved the mining right the day before.

Now that expert has spoken out for the first time. Jan Briers headed up the DMR’s Environmental Section and evaluated the mine’s application.
27:30
Jan: I didn’t recommend the mining to go ahead. There were serious flaws, a number of them.

V/O: Most alarmingly, Jan claims that the mine’s own specialists didn’t support the project.
29:00
Jan: They are careful in what they say. If they don’t support it they say this can go wrong, but they don’t make decisions for you, they leave the decision up to you.

John: So, what are you trying to tell me now?

Jan: It’s there: the specialists didn’t recommend it.

John: Their own specialists?

Jan: Ja.

Link: The Kropz Head Office is in the manicured surrounds of a made-to-order business park on the outskirts of Cape Town. It’s about as far removed as you’re likely to get from the West Coast National Park and the Elandsfontein Mine, which we were hoping to get an on-camera update on. But Kropz said that they would respond to our questions in writing.

V/O: Mr Brier’s comments refer to the draft submission in June 2014, and not the final submission.
None of the specialist studies that the Environmental Assessment Practitioner obtained indicated that the project was not supported.

V/O: Kropz started excavating last August - 10 months before they had a Water Use License. Satellite imagery taken in January shows water in the two reservoirs, holding tanks and the excavation pit. Zero rainfall was recorded in the Langebaan area that month, yet photographs show groundwater in the pit. Groundwater can also be seen in this Kropz corporate video shot in February. It is alleged that when the Water Use License was issued in April, Kropz was already in contravention of the License. But Kropz say:

V/O: We stopped mining above the water table. Small volumes of ground water seeped into the pit and accumulated there until we had permission to pump.

At no point did we proceed without the necessary permits and permissions in place.


Carika: There was a previous PPP when they did the initial scoping reports and we all handed in commentary, we never received anything back again. There were no meetings, to this day there are various farmers who live within a 10km radius of the mine that have never been consulted with.

V/O: Carika van Zyl represents the West Coast Environmental Protection Association.

Carika: If something happens what is our contingency plan? What are we going to do if the aquifer gets polluted? What is the size of the aquifer, what is the shape of the aquifer? Those things still remain unknown.

Walter: We’ve lodged an appeal with the Water Tribunal against the Water Use License decision. In terms of the National Water Act that automatically suspends the Water Use License, unless the Minister directs otherwise.

V/O: Walter Anderson is the lawyer representing the West Coast Environmental Protection Association.

Walter: The appeal has been lodged, it’s been received, it has a case number. So, it’s been suspended, and we have received no directive from the Minister to say otherwise. But the Mine is still dewatering. It is still conducting water use activities, without which they cannot mine.

V/O: Ironically Kropz suspended mining operations in July, citing technical difficulties and the drop in the price of phosphate. When development began in 2009, it was over $400 per ton. Today it’s $85. This recent footage shows the extent of their excavations. The softs stockpile has grown massively, while the water reservoirs show that dewatering is continuing. But this R1.5billion mine is deserted, as most of the workforce has been laid off. The 450 jobs promised, have evaporated.


Carika: And this is after they’ve said they’ve spent R25 million on getting the best available experts, now they are in. They’ve made this 1.8km by 800 metres by 50 metres deep hole in the ground, and now they’re running into problems.

Link: In their brief responses to our questions Kropz blame many of their difficulties, including the job losses at the mine, their technical difficulties in accessing all of their phosphate ore, as well as their financial problems on the delay in issuing their Water Usage License.

V/O: They have promised to re-employ the previous employees as soon as possible.

V/O: So, who is Kropz? Kropz was founded by South African mining entrepreneur, Mike Nunn, the man who pioneered the tanzanite industry. Kropz International is registered in the corporate tax haven of Luxembourg, while Nunn resides in the individual tax haven of Monaco.

25% of Kropz is owned by African Rainbow Capital, which recently listed on the JSE. The Chairman is Dr Patrice Motsepe, and Executive Director is Dr Johan van Zyl, who is also Chairman of Sanlam. They weren’t available for interviews regarding the controversy, but we received this written response:

Text: Neither Kropz nor ARC, has been informed by the competent authority that the license has been suspended. Neither Dr Johan van Zyl nor Dr Patrice Motsepe has sanctioned any unlawful action in respect of Kropz.
V/O: In Parliament last month, the Department of Water and Sanitation stated:
No, the Minister has not authorised Kropz to undertake listed water use despite the suspension of its water use licence as a result of an appeal pending before the Water Tribunal.”
Link: The Elandsfontein Aquifer is a massive fresh water resource that runs for miles underground. The Saldanha Bay Municipality has a plan to tap into that aquifer as the continuing drought threatens the collapse of local industry. It’s hoping to piggyback on the mine’s infrastructure, and in so doing avoid the lengthy environmental impact process.

Andre: We cannot stand by and just say that the source, the aquifer, is there and the infrastructure already laid down by the mine must just be ignored in the possibility of solutions for this crisis situation

V/O: According to Andre Kruger, the Municipality agreed to supply the mine with 1 .6 million litres of potable water per day. But with Level 4 water restrictions already in place, it’s just as well that mining is suspended.

John: Would you still be able to meet the mine’s requirements if they were fully operational?

Andre: Well, we wouldn’t be able to meet any of the industries’ requirements.

V/O: That is why they are pinning their hopes on the aquifer water.

Andre: What is going to happen on Day Zero in January and February next year when there is no water in the region, and we have to supply water domestically, and we have to supply water to keep the economy going.

V/O: They have appointed experts to measure the feasibility and environmental impact of diverting aquifer water to the municipality, but is it legal?

Walter: Reinjection was a material condition for this Water Use Licence being granted, and the municipality is proposing to remove that condition and take that water. The mine will receive water from the aquifer, that was previously prohibited. That is what will effectively happen because the municipality will take that water directly from the aquifer and give it directly to the mine.

V/O: Not so, says Kropz:

Text: “Kropz would not benefit in any way from providing water to the municipality, but welcomes the opportunity to assist the Saldanha Bay Municipality and the community.”

John: And you would need another Water Use License?

Andre: We have to get another Water Use License for that. We’ve spoken to the Department of Water and Sanitation and asked whether we would be able to use that aquifer at any time. They’ve brought it to our attention that there is an appeal, and it would not be available in the short term. But it is something that can still be considered.

V/O: So why was the Municipality informed about the appeal, but not Kropz? We asked the Department for comment, but received no answer. The West Coast Environmental Association has now applied to the Cape High Court for an urgent interdict to stop Kropz from dewatering the aquifer. In a media release Kropz says if they stop,

V/O: “The pit will flood… negatively impacting groundwater.”

V/O: Kropz will oppose the application, but the Minister of Water & Sanitation and her Department will not.

Carika: This is a fight worth fighting. I will not, we will not stop until we’ve been at the highest Court, because so many rights and regulations are just being violated with a smile.
